newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch pension revolution puts onus on individual.
newsitem.headline: Dutch pension revolution puts onus on individual.

text.p: The Dutch, among the most frugal people in Europe, are being forced to take more responsibility for their retirement income as their pension fund industry is revolutionised.

The Dutch government is reforming the state pension system to cap soaring costs while private, company employee pension funds are also under pressure to make changes to cope with the effects of an ageing population, industry officials said.
"I think it's a revolution," said Jan Tamerus, chief actuary with the health services industry fund PGGM.
He said that for the first time state and private pension funds were bucking the trend of raising premiums in the face of spiralling liabilities.
The Netherlands, with a population of only 15 million, has about 1,100 pension funds managing 800 billion guilders.
Among them is ABP, the world's second biggest pension fund, which manages 250 billion guilders of civil servants savings.
"The Dutch, historically, haven't been high spenders. We've been big savers," said one pension fund manager.
Gross national saving in 1995 was 24.6 percent of nominal gross domestic product, higher than most European nations.
Industry officials attribute the high savings rate to compulsory membership of occupational funds.

But they said people were increasingly diverting additional savings to their own private pension plans, managed by external parties such as insurance companies, as state and occupational schemes became less generous.
"People are much more responsible for their savings and for their pensions. It's much more individualised and flexible," he said.
As an example, he said workers may have the option of retiring at 60 instead of 65 but still collecting a pension.

Consultant Henk Klein Haneveld said the ageing population was boosting costs for Dutch pension funds, forcing them to hire external managers and increase their weightings in equities to achieve higher returns to meet spiralling liabilities.
The proportion of Dutch people aged 65-plus is forecast to rise to 23 percent by 2035 from 13 percent now.
"The ratio between dependent pensioners and contribution paying active members is worsening. Funds are more conscious of the efficiency of their operations," he said.
About 25 to 30 percent of Dutch pension savings are invested in shares, up from five to 10 percent in the early 1980s.
Toine van der Stee, the Robeco group's managing director for institutional asset management in the Netherlands, sees the weighting of shares growing to between 40 and 60 percent.
"They're looking for higher-yielding assets. Most pension funds will shift toward equities," he said.

Facing spiralling costs due to the "greying" of the population, the Dutch government plans to cap workers' contributions toward the state pension at 15.4 percent of pay, a rate which has risen from 10.8 percent since 1989.

The government is also encouraging occupational schemes to base retirement pensions on average, rather than final wages. This would limit the revenues it loses as a result of the tax-deductibility of premiums and keep premiums down.
"At the moment, there's a lot of attention on pensions. You see that in politics," said Cees Verhagen, communications officer with pension and insurance watchdog, Vezekeringskamer.
Party officials of the governing coalition have also suggested starting a system of partial capital funding of age pensions whereby one billion guilders a year would be invested for future pensions.
Under the present system, state retirement pensions are paid out of premiums contributed by the current workforce.
Verhagen said occupational pension funds were drawing a larger proportion of their income from investment income than annual premiums as they raised their exposure to shares.
"With higher (investment) profits, they can offer employers and employees lower premiums," he said.
He said company and industry-wide pension schemes might even make membership voluntary over the next five to 10 years, allowing employees them to make their own arrangements.
Dutch employers body, the VNO-NCW, said collective pension schemes currently managed about 600 million guilders of funds and this was expected to leap to 1,000 billion guilders by 2010.
PGGM's Tamerus said compulsory schemes were considering allowing members more flexibility to organise their own pensions as funds sought to curb the rise in premiums.
"They have to do more for themselves to make up the difference," he said.
This was expected to give insurers a larger slice of the pension market, prompting occupational funds like ABP and PGGM to establish their own insurance subsidiaries, he said.
